results.title: MCP Server
excerpts:
# MCP Server

> Connect AI assistants to your Twenty workspace using the Model Context Protocol.

## Overview

Twenty exposes an [MCP](modelcontextprotocol.io/) server so that AI assistants — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, and others — can read and write your CRM data through natural language.

Use your **workspace URL** (the URL you use to access Twenty) as the MCP endpoint. On Twenty Cloud, your workspace URL might be `{mycompany}.twenty.com` or a custom domain. The server is available at:

| Environment | MCP Endpoint |
| - | - |
| **Cloud** | `{your-workspace-url}/mcp` (e.g. `mycompany.twenty.com/mcp`) |
| **Self-Hosted** | `{your-domain}/mcp` |

## Authentication Methods

You have two ways to authenticate your MCP client: **OAuth** (recommended) or **API Key**.

### Option A — OAuth (Recommended)

With OAuth, your MCP client opens a browser window for you to log in. No secrets are stored in config files, and tokens refresh automatically.

> [!NOTE]
>
> OAuth requires an MCP client that supports the [MCP Authorization specification](modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/authorization). Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, and ChatGPT support it.

Add this to your MCP client configuration, replacing `{your-workspace-url}` with your workspace host (e.g. `mycompany.twenty.com`):

```json theme={null}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "twenty": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "{your-workspace-url}/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

That's it — no API key needed. When the client connects for the first time it will:

1. Discover Twenty's OAuth metadata via `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` and `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`
2. Register itself as an OAuth client via dynamic client registration (RFC 7591)
3. Open your browser to authorize access
4. Receive tokens and connect to the MCP server

Subsequent connections reuse the stored tokens and refresh them automatically.

### Option B — API Key

If your MCP client does not support OAuth, or you prefer static credentials, pass an API key in the `Authorization` header:

```json theme={null}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "twenty": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "{your-workspace-url}/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> Your API key grants access to workspace data. Keep it out of version control and shared dotfiles.

To create an API key, go to **Settings → Developers → API → + Create key**. See [APIs](docs.twenty.com/developers/extend/api.md#create-an-api-key) for details.

## Quick Start

### 1. Copy the config

Go to **Settings → AI → MCP** in Twenty. Choose your authentication method (OAuth or API Key), copy the JSON snippet (it will already use your workspace URL), and paste it into your MCP client's config file.

...

### 2. Connect

Restart your MCP client (or reload the config). If using OAuth you will be redirected to Twenty to authorize access. If using an API key the connection is immediate.

### 3. Start using it

Ask your AI assistant to interact with your CRM:

* *"Show me the 5 most recently created companies"*
* *"Create a new person named Jane Doe at Acme Corp"*
* *"Find all open opportunities worth more than \$10k"*

## Available Tools

Once connected, the MCP server lists the same tools in every workspace:

* **Record tools** take the object as an argument: `find_records`, `group_records`, `create_records`, `update_record`, `update_records`, `upsert_records`, `delete_records` and `merge_records`. For example, `find_records({ objectName: "company", select: ["name"] })`.
* **Discovery tools** tell the assistant what your workspace contains: `list_object_metadata_names` for objects and `get_field_metadata` for the fields of an object.

...

The list holds about a hundred tool definitions. Clients that load tools on demand, as Claude, Claude Code, Codex and ChatGPT do by default, handle it well. A client that loads every tool definition up front can use a large part of its context: connect it to meta mode instead.

### Direct mode

Connect to `/mcp?mode=direct` to list one tool per object and operation instead, each with the exact input schema of that object: `find_many_companies`, `create_one_person`, and several hundred more. Direct mode also lists the other built-in tools, the functions of your installed apps and the tools of your connected MCP servers. Tools for objects created while you are connected appear after reconnecting.

This needs a client that loads tools on demand, as Claude, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode do by default. A client that loads every tool definition up front, including Claude Code with tool search turned off, can run out of context.

excerpts:
# APIs

> REST and GraphQL APIs generated from your workspace schema.

## Schema-per-tenant APIs

There is no static API reference for Twenty. Each workspace has its own schema — when you add a custom object (say `Invoice`), it immediately gets REST and GraphQL endpoints identical to built-in objects like `Company` or `Person`. The API is generated from the schema, so endpoints use your object and field names directly — no opaque IDs.

Your workspace-specific API documentation is available under **Settings → Developers → API** after creating an API key. It includes an interactive playground where you can execute real calls against your data.

## Two APIs

**Core API** — `/rest/` and `/graphql/`

CRUD on records: People, Companies, Opportunities, your custom objects. Query, filter, traverse relations.

**Metadata API** — `/rest/metadata/` and `/metadata/`

Schema management: create/modify/delete objects, fields, and relations. This is how you programmatically change your data model.

Both are available as REST and GraphQL. GraphQL adds batch upserts and the ability to traverse relations in a single query. Same underlying data either way.

...

## Authentication

```
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
```

Create an API key in **Settings → Developers → API → + Create key**. Copy it immediately — it's shown once. Keys can be scoped to a specific role under **Settings → Members → Roles → Assignment tab** to limit what they can access.

[Creating API key](player.vimeo.com/video/928786722?autoplay=1\&loop=1\&autopause=0\&background=1\&app_id=58479)

For OAuth-based access (external apps acting on behalf of users), see [OAuth](docs.twenty.com/developers/extend/oauth.md).

## Batch operations

Both REST and GraphQL support batching up to 60 records per request — create, update, or delete. GraphQL also supports batch upsert (create-or-update in one call) using plural names like `CreateCompanies`.

## Selecting fields (REST)

REST record endpoints accept a `fields` query parameter to return only the fields you need:

```
GET /rest/people?fields=id,name,emails,company
```

excerpts:
API

​

Overview
The Twenty API allows developers to interact programmatically with the Twenty CRM platform. Using the API, you can integrate Twenty with other systems, automate data synchronization, and build custom solutions around your customer data. The API provides endpoints to create, read, update, and delete core CRM objects (such as people and companies) as well as access metadata configuration. API Playground: You can now access the API Playground within the app’s settings. To try out API calls in real-time, log in to your Twenty workspace and navigate to Settings → APIs & Webhooks . This opens the in-app API Playground and the settings for API keys. Go to API Settings

...

Authentication
Twenty’s API uses API keys for authentication. Every request to protected endpoints must include an API key in the header.
* API Keys: You can generate a new API key from your Twenty app’s API settings page. Each API key is a secret token that grants access to your CRM data, so keep it safe. If a key is compromised, revoke it from the settings and generate a new one.
* Auth Header: Once you have an API key, include it in the Authorization header of your HTTP requests. Use the Bearer token scheme. For example:
Copy
Ask AI
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
Replace YOUR_API_KEY with the key you obtained. This header must be present on all API requests . If the token is missing or invalid, the API will respond with an authentication error (HTTP 401 Unauthorized).

...

API Endpoints
All resources can be accessed and via REST or GraphQL.
* Cloud: api.twenty.com/ or your custom domain / sub-domain
* Self-Hosted Instances: If you are running Twenty on your own server, use your own domain in place of api.twenty.com (for example, {your-domain}/rest/ ).
Endpoints are grouped into two categories: Core API and Metadata API . The Core API deals with primary CRM data (e.g. people, companies, notes, tasks), while the Metadata API covers configuration data (like custom fields or object definitions). Most integrations will primarily use the Core API.

​

Core API
Accessed on /rest/ or /graphql/ . The Core API serves as a unified interface for managing core CRM entities (people, companies, notes, tasks) and their relationships, offering both REST and GraphQL interaction models.

...

Metadata API
Accessed on /rest/metadata/ or /metadata/ . The Metadata API endpoints allow you to retrieve information about your schema and settings. For instance, you can fetch definitions of custom fields, object schemas, etc.
* Example Endpoints:
* GET /rest/metadata/objects – List all object types and their metadata (fields, relationships).
* GET /rest/metadata/objects/{objectName} – Get metadata for a specific object (e.g., people , companies ).
* GET /rest/metadata/picklists – Retrieve picklist (dropdown) field options defined in the CRM.
Typically, the metadata endpoints are used to understand the structure of data (for dynamic integrations or form-building) rather than to manage actual records. They are read-only in most cases. Authentication is required for these as well (use your API key).

results.title: OAuth
excerpts:
# OAuth

> Authorization code flow with PKCE and client credentials for server-to-server access.

## Overview

Twenty implements OAuth 2.0 with authorization code + PKCE for user-facing apps and client credentials for server-to-server access. Clients are registered dynamically via [RFC 7591](datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7591) — no manual setup in a dashboard.

## When to Use OAuth

| Scenario | Auth Method |
| - | - |
| Internal scripts, automation | [API Key](docs.twenty.com/developers/extend/api.md#authentication) |
| External app acting on behalf of a user | **OAuth — Authorization Code** |
| Server-to-server, no user context | **OAuth — Client Credentials** |
| Twenty App with UI extensions | [Apps](docs.twenty.com/developers/extend/apps/getting-started/quick-start.md) (OAuth is handled automatically) |

## Register a Client

Twenty supports **dynamic client registration** per [RFC 7591](datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7591). No manual setup needed — register programmatically:

```bash theme={null}
POST /oauth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "client_name": "My Integration",
  "redirect_uris": ["myapp.com/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_post"
}
```

**Response:**

```json theme={null}
{
  "client_id": "abc123",
  "client_secret": "secret456",
  "client_name": "My Integration",
  "redirect_uris": ["myapp.com/callback"]
}
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> Store the `client_secret` securely — it cannot be retrieved later.

## Scopes

| Scope | Access |
| - | - |
| `api` | Full read/write access to the Core and Metadata APIs |
| `profile` | Read the authenticated user's profile information |

Request scopes as a space-separated string: `scope=api profile`

## Authorization Code Flow

Use this flow when your app acts on behalf of a Twenty user.

### 1. Redirect the user to authorize

```
GET /oauth/authorize?
  client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
  response_type=code&
  redirect_uri=myapp.com/callback&
  scope=api&
  state=random_state_value&
  code_challenge=CHALLENGE&
  code_challenge_method=S256
```

| Parameter | Required | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `client_id` | Yes | Your registered client ID |
| `response_type` | Yes | Must be `code` |
| `redirect_uri` | Yes | Must match a registered redirect URI |
| `scope` | No | Space-separated scopes (defaults to `api`) |
| `state` | Recommended | Random string to prevent CSRF attacks |
| `code_challenge` | Recommended | PKCE challenge (SHA-256 hash of verifier, base64url-encoded) |
| `code_challenge_method` | Recommended | Must be `S256` when using PKCE |

The user sees a consent screen and approves or denies access.

### 2. Handle the callback

After authorization, Twenty redirects back to your `redirect_uri`:

```
myapp.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE&state=random_state_value
```

Verify that `state` matches what you sent.

### 3. Exchange the code for tokens

```bash theme={null}
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&
code=AUTH_CODE&
redirect_uri=myapp.com/callback&
client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET&
code_verifier=YOUR_PKCE_VERIFIER
```

**Response:**

```json theme={null}
{
  "access_token": "eyJhbG...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "dGhpcyBpcyBh..."
}
```

### 4. Use the access token

```bash theme={null}
GET /rest/companies
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

### 5. Refresh when expired

```bash theme={null}
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&
refresh_token=YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN&
client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

## Client Credentials Flow

For server-to-server integrations with no user interaction:

```bash theme={null}
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&
client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET&
scope=api
```

The returned token has workspace-level access, not tied to any specific user.

## Server Discovery

Twenty publishes its OAuth configuration at a standard discovery endpoint:

```
GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
```

This returns all endpoints, supported grant types, scopes, and capabilities — useful for building generic OAuth clients.

## API Endpoints Summary

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| - | - |
| `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | Server metadata discovery |
| `/oauth/register` | Dynamic client registration |
| `/oauth/authorize` | User authorization |
| `/oauth/token` | Token exchange and refresh |

...

## OAuth vs API Keys

| | API Keys | OAuth |
| - | - | - |
| **Setup** | Generate in Settings | Register a client, implement flow |
| **User context** | None (workspace-level) | Specific user's permissions |
| **Best for** | Scripts, internal tools | External apps, multi-user integrations |
| **Token rotation** | Manual | Automatic via refresh tokens |
| **Scoped access** | Full API access | Granular via scopes |


This documentation is built and hosted on [Mintlify](mintlify.com), a developer documentation platform.

results.title: Securing your instance
excerpts:
Split your instance into three zones:
* Zone | Paths | Who can reach it
* Private | Everything else: the app, /graphql, /rest, /metadata, files | Your team only
* Public | /webhooks, /s, /emailing | Anyone. These are called by services that can't join your network.
* Cloud AI connectors | /mcp, /oauth, /.well-known | Anthropic and OpenAI IP ranges. Any of their users can reach these paths, but only your team can log in.
Each path covers everything under it. Open the public and cloud AI zones only if you use the features behind them, see Public paths. Otherwise, keep the whole instance private. AI assistants that run on your team's computers, like Claude Code, need nothing opened, see AI clients.
[!NOTE]
What you give up: hosted automation tools that call the Twenty API from their own cloud (Zapier, Make, n8n Cloud) can't reach a private instance. Run them inside your network instead (self-hosted n8n works well), or use Twenty workflows.

...

* Email links can only record an open, a click or an unsubscribe for the recipient they were sent to.

AI clients (MCP)

AI assistants are one of the main ways your team will use Twenty, through its MCP server. What you need to open depends on where the assistant runs, not on which assistant it is.

Local clients: nothing to open

Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor and other tools that run on your computer connect to Twenty from that computer. If it's on your tailnet or VPN, they reach /mcp the same way your browser reaches the app. This is the safest setup, so prefer it when you can.
Claude Desktop is the exception: connectors added in Settings → Connectors run in Anthropic's cloud, even in the desktop app. To keep the connection local, add Twenty as a local MCP server in claude_desktop_config.json instead:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "twenty": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "mcp-remote",
        "twenty.your-tailnet.ts.net/mcp"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Cloud connectors: open with care

Claude (web, mobile, and connectors in the desktop app) and ChatGPT call your server from Anthropic's and OpenAI's infrastructure, not from your device. They can't reach a private instance, so you have to open /mcp, /oauth and /.well-known to their IP ranges.
[!WARNING]
An IP allowlist checks which network a request comes from, not who sent it. Anyone with a Claude or ChatGPT account can add your URL as a connector and send requests to these paths.
What keeps them out is login. To get a token, a user has to sign in on Twenty's /authorize page, which stays in the private zone. Someone outside your network can start the connection flow but can't finish it, and /mcp rejects every request without a valid token.
What stays exposed is the code that runs before login: OAuth discovery, client registration (/oauth/register) and the token endpoint. The allowlist narrows that: internet-wide scanners can't reach these paths directly, and requests have to come through Claude's or ChatGPT's infrastructure. It doesn't make that code safe on its own, so upgrades still matter.
If you use cloud connectors:
* Open only /mcp, /oauth and /.well-known. Never open /authorize or the rest of the app.
* Allow only the vendors you use:
* Anthropic: 160.79.104.0/21, from Anthropic's IP addresses page.
* OpenAI: the list in chatgpt-connectors.json. OpenAI describes it as best effort and it changes over time, so refresh it on a schedule:
curl -s openai.com/chatgpt-connectors.json | jq -r '.prefixes[].ipv4Prefix | select(.)'
* Upgrade quickly when release notes mention MCP or OAuth fixes.

Logic functions

sources.title: OAuth - Twenty Documentation
sources.trimmed:
## Overview

Twenty implements OAuth 2.0 with authorization code + PKCE for user-facing apps and client credentials for server-to-server access. Clients are registered dynamically via RFC 7591 — no manual setup in a dashboard.

## When to Use OAuth

| Scenario | Auth Method |
| --- | --- |
| Internal scripts, automation | API Key |
| External app acting on behalf of a user | **OAuth — Authorization Code** |
| Server-to-server, no user context | **OAuth — Client Credentials** |
| Twenty App with UI extensions | Apps (OAuth is handled automatically) |

## Register a Client

Twenty supports **dynamic client registration** per RFC 7591. No manual setup needed — register programmatically:

```
POST /oauth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "client_name": "My Integration",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://myapp.com/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "client_secret_post"
}
```

**Response:**

```
{
  "client_id": "abc123",
  "client_secret": "secret456",
  "client_name": "My Integration",
  "redirect_uris": ["https://myapp.com/callback"]
}
```

Store the `client_secret` securely — it cannot be retrieved later.

## Scopes

| Scope | Access |
| --- | --- |
| `api` | Full read/write access to the Core and Metadata APIs |
| `profile` | Read the authenticated user’s profile information |

Request scopes as a space-separated string: `scope=api profile`

## Authorization Code Flow

Use this flow when your app acts on behalf of a Twenty user.

### 1. Redirect the user to authorize

```
GET /oauth/authorize?
  client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
  response_type=code&
  redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/callback&
  scope=api&
  state=random_state_value&
  code_challenge=CHALLENGE&
  code_challenge_method=S256
```

| Parameter | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `client_id` | Yes | Your registered client ID |
| `response_type` | Yes | Must be `code` |
| `redirect_uri` | Yes | Must match a registered redirect URI |
| `scope` | No | Space-separated scopes (defaults to `api`) |
| `state` | Recommended | Random string to prevent CSRF attacks |
| `code_challenge` | Recommended | PKCE challenge (SHA-256 hash of verifier, base64url-encoded) |
| `code_challenge_method` | Recommended | Must be `S256` when using PKCE |

The user sees a consent screen and approves or denies access.

### 2. Handle the callback

After authorization, Twenty redirects back to your `redirect_uri`:

```
https://myapp.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE&state=random_state_value
```

Verify that `state` matches what you sent.

### 3. Exchange the code for tokens

```
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&
code=AUTH_CODE&
redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/callback&
client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET&
code_verifier=YOUR_PKCE_VERIFIER
```

**Response:**

```
{
  "access_token": "eyJhbG...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "dGhpcyBpcyBh..."
}
```

### 4. Use the access token

```
GET /rest/companies
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

### 5. Refresh when expired

```
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&
refresh_token=YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN&
client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

## Client Credentials Flow

For server-to-server integrations with no user interaction:

```
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&
client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET&
scope=api
```

The returned token has workspace-level access, not tied to any specific user.

## Server Discovery

Twenty publishes its OAuth configuration at a standard discovery endpoint:

```
GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
```

This returns all endpoints, supported grant types, scopes, and capabilities — useful for building generic OAuth clients.

## API Endpoints Summary

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | ---

sources.title: MCP Server - Twenty Documentation
sources.trimmed:
## Overview

Twenty exposes an MCP server so that AI assistants — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, and others — can read and write your CRM data through natural language.
Use your **workspace URL** (the URL you use to access Twenty) as the MCP endpoint. On Twenty Cloud, your workspace URL might be `https://{mycompany}.twenty.com` or a custom domain. The server is available at:


| Environment | MCP Endpoint |
| --- | --- |
| **Cloud** | `https://{your-workspace-url}/mcp` (e.g. `https://mycompany.twenty.com/mcp`) |
| **Self-Hosted** | `https://{your-domain}/mcp` |

The endpoint speaks MCP protocol `2026-07-28` and the earlier revisions back to `2024-11-05` over Streamable HTTP. Clients on `2026-07-28` call `server/discover` and send each request on its own; older clients start with `initialize` as before.

## Authentication Methods

You have two ways to authenticate your MCP client: **OAuth** (recommended) or **API Key**.
With OAuth, your MCP client opens a browser window for you to log in. No secrets are stored in config files, and tokens refresh automatically.

OAuth requires an MCP client that supports the MCP Authorization specification. Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, and ChatGPT support it.

Add this to your MCP client configuration, replacing `{your-workspace-url}` with your workspace host (e.g. `mycompany.twenty.com`):

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "twenty": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://{your-workspace-url}/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

That’s it — no API key needed. When the client connects for the first time it will:

1. Discover Twenty’s OAuth metadata via `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` and `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`
2. Register itself as an OAuth client via dynamic client registration (RFC 7591)
3. Open your browser to authorize access
4. Receive tokens and connect to the MCP server

Subsequent connections reuse the stored tokens and refresh them automatically.

### Option B — API Key

If your MCP client does not support OAuth, or you prefer static credentials, pass an API key in the `Authorization` header:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "twenty": {
      "type": "streamable-http",
      "url": "https://{your-workspace-url}/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Your API key grants access to workspace data. Keep it out of version control and shared dotfiles.

To create an API key, go to **Settings → Developers → API → + Create key**. See APIs for details.

## Quick Start

### 1. Copy the config

Go to **Settings → AI → MCP** in Twenty. Choose your authentication method (OAuth or API Key), copy the JSON snippet (it will already use your workspace URL), and paste it into your MCP client’s config file.


| Client | Config file location |
| --- | --- |
| **Claude Desktop** | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS) or `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` (Windows) |
| **Claude Code** | `~/.claude.json` (user) or `.mcp.json` (project) |
| **Cursor** | `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` globally |
| **ChatGPT** | Turn on Developer Mode in **Settings → Apps & Connectors → Advanced settings**, then use **Create** in **Settings → Apps & Connectors** to add the MCP server |

### 2. Connect

Restart your MCP client (or reload the config). If using OAuth you will be redirected to Twenty to authorize access. If using an API key the connection is immediate.

### 3. Start using it

Ask your AI assistant to interact with your CRM:

* *“Show me the 5 most recently created companies”*
* *“Create a new person named Jane Doe at Acme Corp”*
* *“Find all open opportunities worth more than $10k”*

## Available Tools

Once connected, the MCP server lists the same tools in every workspace:

* **Record tools** take the object as an argument: `find_records`, `group_records`, `create_records`, `update_record`, `update_records`, `upsert_records`, `delete_records`
